name: Battle of Kursk
info: In the summer of 1943 German forces attacked the Kursk salient on the Eastern Front, were stopped by deep Soviet defences, and were then driven back by Soviet counter-offensives that left the Red Army holding the strategic initiative.

facts.date: 5 July to 23 August 1943: the German offensive, Operation Citadel, began on 5 July and was ended on 17 July in the south; the Soviet counter-offensives began on 12 July and 3 August, and Kharkov was liberated on 23 August
facts.place: The Kursk salient, near Kursk in south-western Russia, with fighting on its northern face at Ponyri and Olkhovatka and on its southern face at Prokhorovka
facts.sides: Nazi Germany under Hitler, with Field Marshal Erich von Manstein (Army Group South) and Field Marshal Günther von Kluge (Army Group Centre), about 777,000 to 779,000 men at the start; the Soviet Union under Stalin, with Zhukov, Vatutin, Rokossovsky and Konev, about 1,910,361 men including the Steppe Front reserve
facts.outcome: The German offensive was halted before it broke through, reaching a depth of 8 to 12 kilometres in the north and 35 kilometres in the south. Soviet counter-offensives at Orel and Kharkov followed, and the Soviets kept the initiative for the rest of the war.

t: Soviet intelligence, from the Lucy spy ring and from decrypts forwarded by John Cairncross, gave the Red Army months of warning, and it built a defence in depth of six belts, with 503,993 anti-tank mines laid.
German losses are hard to fix: Frieser counts 54,182 casualties during Citadel itself, while other historians put losses over the whole battle at 380,000 to 430,000 or more than half a million.
Hitler ended the offensive after a week, in part because the Western Allies had invaded Sicily, and Germany never launched another major offensive on the Eastern Front.
dyk: On 8 July German ground-attack aircraft armed with 30 mm MK 103 cannon destroyed at least 50 tanks of the Soviet 2nd Guards Tank Corps, the first time in military history that an attacking tank formation was defeated by air power alone.
ev: Kursk is retaken by the Soviets on 8 February, and Manstein's counter-stroke later retakes Kharkov and Belgorod, leaving a Soviet salient centred on Kursk
Hitler orders Operation Citadel on 15 April, and Stalin and the Stavka agree to defend first and counterattack afterwards
The German offensive opens on the northern and southern faces of the salient
The Western Allies invade Sicily, and the German advance in the north is halted
The Soviets launch Operation Kutuzov, and the armoured clash at Prokhorovka is fought on the southern face
Operation Roland ends and the II SS Panzer Corps is ordered to withdraw
Operation Polkovodets Rumyantsev opens against the southern wing of Army Group South
Kharkov is liberated after heavy fighting

sections.background:
After the Battle of Stalingrad the Red Army went over to a general offensive in the south. Kursk was retaken by the Soviets on 8 February 1943, but Field Marshal Erich von Manstein, given freedom of action, counterattacked from 21 February and retook Kharkov on 15 March and Belgorod on 18 March. The spring rasputitsa and the exhaustion of both armies ended operations by mid-March, leaving a Soviet salient about 250 kilometres from north to south and 160 kilometres from east to west, centred on Kursk.

On 15 April Hitler issued Operational Order No. 6, calling for the offensive codenamed Zitadelle (Citadel). It was meant to weaken Soviet offensive strength for the summer, and Hitler believed a victory would restore German prestige with allies he thought were considering withdrawing from the war. It was also hoped that many Soviet prisoners would be taken for use as slave labour in German armaments factories. Model, Guderian and later Manstein doubted it, and Hitler postponed it several times to wait for new tanks, until 5 July.

The Soviet side knew of the plan. The Lucy spy ring in Switzerland passed on intelligence, which John Cairncross confirmed by forwarding raw decrypts from Bletchley Park. Stalin and some officers wished to strike first, but Zhukov and others advised a strategic defensive. In April Stalin and the Stavka agreed to wear out the German attack before counterattacking.
sections.forces:
The German force amounted to around 777,000 men, 2,451 tanks and assault guns, which was 70 percent of the German armour on the Eastern Front, and 7,417 guns and mortars. By another count the total was 777,000 to 779,000 men. In the north Model's 9th Army had 335,000 men and 988 tanks and assault guns. In the south Hoth's 4th Panzer Army and Army Detachment Kempf, under Werner Kempf, had 1,377. About 259 Panthers, 211 Tigers and 90 Ferdinands were used. The force was markedly short of infantry, and the Panthers came straight from training, with little time to learn the terrain.

The Soviets prepared three main defensive belts in each of the Central Front's and Voronezh Front's sectors, backed by three fallback belts, with the whole system nearly 300 kilometres deep, including lines manned by the Steppe Front. More than 300,000 civilians worked on it. The engineers laid 503,993 anti-tank and 439,348 anti-personnel mines. Nearly all artillery was given an anti-tank role, and infantry were trained against 'tank phobia' by having tanks driven over them in trenches.

The Central Front under Rokossovsky held the northern face, the Voronezh Front under Vatutin the southern, and Konev's Steppe Front was in reserve. Soviet strength was 1,910,361 men, of whom 1,426,352 were combat soldiers, and 4,869 tanks and 259 self-propelled guns. About a third of the tanks were light. The T-34's 76.2 mm gun struggled against the frontal armour of Tigers and Panthers.
sections.course:
Fighting began on the evening of 4 July on the southern face, and Zhukov ordered a pre-emptive bombardment at around 02:00 on 5 July, which delayed the Germans but did not disrupt their schedule. The Germans attacked on both faces that morning. In the north Model used infantry divisions reinforced with assault guns and heavy tanks, keeping his panzer divisions back for exploitation. Minefields slowed them, and by the end of the first day they had advanced 5 to 6 miles at a cost of 1,287 killed and missing and 5,921 wounded. Fighting then centred on Ponyri and Olkhovatka for three days. By 10 July the Soviets had halted the advance.

In the south the main attack was delivered by Hoth's 4th Panzer Army. The II SS Panzer Corps broke through the first Soviet belt by 09:00 on 5 July, but the 3rd SS Division made slow progress and Army Detachment Kempf was delayed at the Donets. Soviet counterattacks on 8 July were piecemeal and failed, but stalled the II SS Panzer Corps. On 9 July German units reached the Psel River, and the corps turned north-east towards Prokhorovka.

On 12 July, at about 08:30, Rotmistrov ordered the 5th Guards Tank Army to attack at Prokhorovka. It failed with heavy losses, though it stopped a German breakthrough, and by the end of the day the Soviets had fallen back to their starting positions. That evening Hitler summoned Kluge and Manstein and stopped the offensive.
sections.aftermath:
Hitler ended the offensive because the Western Allies had invaded Sicily two days earlier and he feared further landings in Italy or southern France. Manstein was reluctant, believing his forces were on the verge of breaking through. Hitler agreed to let the southern attack go on, then moved Manstein's reserve south. Operation Roland began on 14 July, and on 17 July the II SS Panzer Corps was ordered to withdraw, one division going to Italy.

On 12 July the Soviets launched Operation Kutuzov against the Orel salient, which threatened Model's 9th Army and forced it onto the defensive. On 3 August Operation Polkovodets Rumyantsev began against the southern wing of Army Group South. The Soviets liberated Belgorod on 5 August and reached the outskirts of Kharkov by 12 August, where a counter-attack by the 2nd and 3rd SS Panzer Divisions halted them. Kharkov was liberated on 23 August.

Krivosheyev's figures, which Glantz considers the most reliable, give Soviet losses of 177,877 in the German offensive. The two Soviet offensives cost 685,456. Frieser calculates 54,182 German casualties during Citadel, and about 170,000 for the three battles. Soviet tank losses were 1,614 of 3,925 during the German offensive. Hitler blamed the defeat on his General Staff.
sections.sources:
Casualty figures are uncertain for both sides. German equipment losses are hard to count because the Germans tried to recover and repair tanks, so a tank disabled one day might be back in action the next. German personnel records were seized at the end of the war; many went to the United States national archives and were not available until 1978, while others were taken by the Soviet Union, which declined to confirm that they existed.

Historians disagree on the Soviet dead. Töppel says official figures are underestimated by 40%, which gives 1.2 million, and cites Russian critics with estimates from 910,000 to 2.3 million. Sokolov gives 450,000 killed, 50,000 missing and 1.2 million wounded, which Glantz says may be inflated, though he accepts that the official figures are probably conservative. Many Russian historians consider Sokolov unreliable. Estimates of German losses over the whole battle range from 380,000 to 430,000 and, per Bellamy and Hastings, more than half a million.

Schönbach argues that Western historians have used German loss statistics without critical analysis, because 'total losses' were recorded as tanks under repair, and that 40% to 50% of German tanks were caught in a repair backlog. Estimates of tanks destroyed vary: Frieser has 760 and Töppel up to 1,200. For aircraft, Frieser calls the official Soviet figure of 1,626 'completely unbelievable' and Bergström counts 1,104 Soviet aircraft lost.
sections.legacy:
The battle was the first time in the Second World War that a German strategic offensive was halted before it could break through enemy defences and penetrate to its strategic depths. It was the last strategic offensive the Germans were able to launch on the Eastern Front. Guderian wrote that the failure of Zitadelle was a decisive defeat, after which the enemy was in undisputed possession of the initiative. The counter-offensives were the Red Army's first successful summer offensives of the war.

Kursk has been called the single largest battle in the history of warfare and the single deadliest armoured battle in history. The opening day, 5 July, was the costliest day in aerial warfare in terms of aircraft shot down. It is cited by some as the true turning point of the European theatre, though this view has frequently been criticised. Robin Cross wrote that Kursk dealt the Ostheer heavier psychological and material blows than Stalingrad.

Hitler's interference in German military matters grew, while Stalin, trusting commanders whose decisions brought success, stepped back from operational planning, so that the Red Army was given more autonomy. A total of 239 Red Army personnel were made Hero of the Soviet Union for the battle, among them two women medics, Mariya Borovichenko and Zinaida Mareseva, posthumously.

summary: At Kursk in July 1943 the Germans attacked a Soviet salient and were halted by deep defences prepared with advance knowledge of the plan. Soviet counter-offensives at Orel and Kharkov followed, and the Red Army kept the initiative thereafter.
references: David M. Glantz, The Battle of Kursk (University Press of Kansas, 2004)
David M. Glantz, The Battle for Kursk 1943: The Soviet General Staff Study (Frank Cass, 1999)
Lloyd Clark, Kursk: The Greatest Battle: Eastern Front 1943 (Headline Publishing Group, 2012)
Karl-Heinz Frieser, Germany and the Second World War: The Eastern Front 1943–1944: The War in the East and on the Neighbouring Fronts (Oxford University Press, 2017)
Steven Newton, Kursk: The German View (Da Capo Press, 2002)
Mark Healy, Zitadelle: The German Offensive Against the Kursk Salient 4–17 July 1943 (History Press, 2010)
notes: The article gives no single end date for the battle as a whole; I used 23 August (Kharkov liberated, end of the second Soviet phase) for the span. The lead names only the opening on 5 July.

Figures disputed or conflicting: German losses (Frieser 54,182 in Citadel; 380,000-430,000; over half a million per Bellamy and Hastings); Soviet losses (Krivosheyev 177,877 in the defensive phase vs Töppel 1.2 million, Sokolov); tanks destroyed (Frieser 760, Töppel 1,200); aircraft (Frieser 524 Luftwaffe; Bergström 681 lost or damaged); the article also says 'Soviet losses roughly three times those of the Germans' and 'roughly 5:1', while Bellamy says about 1.5 to 1 in casualties.

Internal inconsistency: Soviet total of 1,910,361 includes the Steppe Front reserve; elsewhere the article says the Soviets massed about 1,300,000 men to defend the salient without the Steppe Front; the 'Comparison of strength' section is empty in the text. The Soviet tank total of 4,869 and the '3,600' figure also differ.
Panthers: the article gives 200 Panthers in two battalions, 259 used in all, and 184 operational on 5 July. I used only the 259 figure.

Left out: the Hero of the Soviet Union detail beyond the count, individual unit actions at Ponyri, Zhukov's and Guderian's quoted passages, air-war statistics, Luftwaffe tank-buster details, the 'mini-Stalingrad' nickname, the Kutuzov and Rumyantsev casualty breakdowns by front, and Maskirovka details.
The Prokhorovka outcome is told as the article does ('neither side accomplished their objectives'); I did not give tank numbers for it because the article gives none for the day.

The legacy section repeats the article's statement that the battle is 'the single largest battle in the history of warfare' as the article's claim, which is a superlative the editor may want to hedge or cut.
Source for the weather and individual anecdotes (Rotmistrov's description of the march, 'ironing' training) is the article only.
